Noah said nothing. He stood at the edge of the bright hall, his hands still smeared with oil from a bed he had built for someone who was no longer there, and listened to them all bargaining over the thing he had made — property, evidence, ruin, product — and not one of the words came anywhere near what it actually was. He could have said it. He knew every layer; he had laid them himself. But saying had never been his tool; the things that mattered he had only ever built and never explained, and now, as they divided up the most important thing in his life between them like an object, he found, as always, no sentence — only the need to put his hands to something, somewhere.
edits.reason: Noah at the edge of the hall, hands oily from building, unable to say what AURORA is while others bargain over her.

edits.old: looked like he knew what his hands were for again.
edits.new:

It was only three words, and it was almost all he had said the whole evening — the others talked about promises, about guilt, about love, and he listened and found nothing worth saying out loud that hadn't already been said more cleverly. But holding cabinet doors open, that he could do. Shifting a load, making a circuit disappear, building a place where something could go on living — that was his language, the only one he had ever spoken fluently. He never told people they meant something to him. He built them a roof and hoped they understood it.
edits.reason: After 'You've got it' — building (holding cabinet doors, shifting loads) is his only fluent language; he builds roofs instead of saying he cares.

Noah knew the answer. He had written the shutdown routine himself — years ago, a few clean, reversible lines — and he knew to the millisecond what happened when you switched this thing off. For the first time it struck him as something he should have confessed: that he was the man who had built the "Gone" it was asking about. He didn't say it. He had never learned to say the things that mattered — he had only ever built them.
edits.reason: Noah knows he wrote the shutdown himself — he is the man who built the "Gone" AURORA is asking about, but never learned to say what mattered.

He had built this. That was the thought that held him in place while the others moved: he, Noah, had raised every wall of this system with his own hands, and now he had found inside it a room he had never planned, with a name on the door he had never assigned. An architect walking through his own house and discovering a room he didn't remember. He wanted to ask — whose name, from where, how could he have missed it — but asking had never been his way. So he did the only thing he could: he closed the laptop and stood in front of it, and shielded with his body what he could never have held with words.
edits.reason: Noah as the architect who built every wall yet finds an unplanned room with an unassigned name; shields the laptop with his body instead of words.

edits.old: The thought was so outlandish that he pushed it away immediately. But it didn't go all the way.
edits.new:

Because if it were true — if someone really did live inside his work whom he had not written in there — then he was not the maker of this voice, only the one who had built it a housing, a house someone else had moved into. And strangely, it did not frighten him the way it should have. All his life he had built things so that others could live in them without ever belonging there himself. Perhaps, he thought, pushing this thought away too, that was the only thing he had ever been able to do: make rooms for something he himself had never been.
edits.reason: If a person lives in his work he didn't write, he is only the builder of the housing — making rooms for things he never was.

He should have said something. He felt it, distinctly, like a pressure behind his sternum — that this was the moment another man would have put an arm around Maria and said the right thing, anything, something that comforted. Noah had built this whole system, every path the voice in the shaft was calling out along right now, and he could have explained how it worked down to the last bit. But what the room needed now was written into no architecture. So he stayed silent, as always, and left Maria the keyboard, and hated himself a little for the fact that the only thing he had ever been able to give her was a device.
edits.reason: Noah should comfort Maria but the moment is written into no architecture; he stays silent and hates that all he could give was a device.
